newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo economists say time ripe for radical reform.
newsitem.headline: Yugo economists say time ripe for radical reform.

text.p: Independent Yugoslav economists called on Monday for radical reforms to bring democracy and an open market economy to the country, shaken by more than two months of protests over local election fraud.

Offering a set of measures to help Yugoslavia out of the economic crisis, 17 experts warned the economy was on the verge of collapse and said the programme was aimed at uncompromised political forces who will best undertake overall reform.

"Protest in Serbia show that Serbians are ready for such radical changes. We have decided to draft such a programme and offer it to all parliamentarian parties, trade unions and chambers of commerce," said Mladjan Dinkic of the Belgrade School of Economics and the key coordinator of the programme.
"The main idea is the need for radical reform and deep political reforms are key to get the country out of the crisis," Dinkic told a news conference.
Economists said that ending talks on division of former Yugoslavia's assets and rejoining world financial institutions were key to the country's economic revival.
"Foreign capital inflow and a quick ending to the talks will be the key to form forex reserves and launch dinar convertibility," Dinkic said.
But to rejoin the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, Yugoslavia will have to meet a set of political conditions and also repay its debts to those institutions.
"Yugoslavia must undergo wide democratisation and probably change its government," Dinkic said.
Only then will talks begin on repaying around $100 million to the IMF and some $1.2 billion to World Bank.
"Debt to the IMF is not so big, but there could be problems with the World Bank," Dinkic said.
And to obtain any fresh lending, Yugoslavia must offer complete internal and external liberalisation, privatisation and macro-economic stabilisation.
The offered programme sees dinar convertibility, supported at first by a $500 million loan from international lenders.

"Citizens would be able to freely buy and sell hard currency in the banks to eliminate the black market. Very soon this loan would be repaid because the stable dinar will attract hard currency," Dinkic said.
"At first the dinar rate would probably be fixed, but soon to become flexible. It depends on what we find at the central bank's books," Dinkic told Reuters.
Economists proposed time-framed, compulsory, transparent and socially-acceptable privatisation.
They called for a ban of all monopolies, ban of all import quotas and a launch of import taxes. "This would support competition and slice inflation," Dinkic added.
The programme envisages re-establishing economic ties with former Yugoslavia's republics.
It proposes an entirely new banking system, a completely independent central bank, and reform in public finances.

Economists called for reallocation of state spending and said the state should spend more to help its poor people than to fight them in the streets, spending three times more on police forces than on agriculture.
The programme will not be offered to the government. "They showed they can't be trusted. Compromised Socialists and leftist parties could not start such a reform," Dinkic said.

The Serbian economy is a catastrophe but economists said the programme could not have been drafted earlier because there was no possibility to feel the pulse of the nation and its need for reforms so openly.

"They're ready for it. People went out on the streets hoping the evil can be stopped. We offer a vision of that hope. An alternative would be hand-to-mouth existence but then we would need 17 years to go back where we were in 1989-90."
Another economics professor Jovan Rankovic insisted there was no more time for patching things up.
"Reform is a must. There is no more time and space to do the patchwork. Inaction would lead us all to death. And nobody wants that. The question is only who undertakes the reform.
"...This programme is the condition for survival of Yugoslav federation," Rankovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
